title: Disasters
hook: after earthquakes and floods, Christians give, rebuild and lament

segments.voice: Yesterday, war: swords into plowshares, and Christians answering it in different ways. Your line was blessed are the peacemakers.

The water has gone down, and it left a line on every wall at the same height. Mud in the kitchen drawers. Photographs drying on a fence. A church parking lot turned into a warehouse of bottled water and diapers, strangers in work gloves passing boxes hand to hand. After a flood, an earthquake, a fire, the same question comes up on the news and at kitchen tables: why did God let this happen? The Bible doesn't give a tidy answer. But it does show what people of faith do next.

First, Jesus refuses one answer. In Luke, he himself brings up a tower that fell in Jerusalem: "Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem? I tell you, Nay." The people under the tower weren't being punished for being worse than everyone else. Whatever a disaster is, the text won't let anyone point at the victims. Then there's lament. Lamentations is a set of poems over a ruined city, and in the middle of the wreckage one line holds on: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Then there's giving. In Acts, a prophet named Agabus warns that a famine is coming, and the response is: "Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea." Not a debate about why. A collection. Then rebuilding. Nehemiah stands before the broken walls of Jerusalem and says, "Come, and let us build up the wall." The people answer, "Let us rise up and build." Lament, give, rebuild. Churches today hold services of mourning after disasters, collect relief, and send crews to tear out wet drywall. The why may never be answered. The text keeps pointing at the next morning, and the next brick.

Bring to mind one place hit recently by a flood, a storm, an earthquake or a fire, and picture one family standing in a doorway there. Hold them for a while without trying to explain anything. If you pray, you can pray the line from Lamentations over them, that his compassions fail not; if you don't, let them stay in your thoughts a little longer.
Disasters. Floods, quakes and fires that the Bible won't blame on the victims, met with lament, with relief, and with people rising up to build.
Your line: rebuild. In Nehemiah, the people answered, let us rise up and build. Day one thousand four hundred six.

howItsDone: After disasters, churches open their buildings as shelters and supply centers, hold services of lament, collect money through their relief agencies, and send volunteers to clean up and rebuild homes.

fork.setup: you're one of the disciples in Antioch. a prophet named Agabus has just warned that a famine is coming, and your brothers and sisters in Judea will go hungry. what do you do?
options: wait to see if the famine really comes.
each give what you can and send relief.
argue about whether the famine is a punishment.
fork.reveal: Acts says every man, according to his ability, determined to send relief to Judea. the answer to a coming disaster was a collection.

chat.says: After the flood back home, people asked if the victims were being punished. What does Jesus say?
options: In Luke he says no: the eighteen killed by the tower weren't worse sinners than anyone.
He never addresses it; the Gospels leave disasters and their victims out entirely.
He says the tower in Siloam fell because its builders had cheated on the work.
chat.meaning: In Luke 13, Jesus asks if the eighteen under the tower in Siloam were worse sinners than everyone in Jerusalem, and answers, I tell you, Nay.

Siloam.meaning: a place in Jerusalem where a tower fell, killing eighteen

Lamentations.meaning: a Bible book of poems over a ruined city

Agabus.meaning: a prophet in Acts who warns that a famine is coming

Nehemiah.meaning: a leader who rallies the people to rebuild Jerusalem's walls

notes: 'eighteen' is spoken because Luke 13:4 says it directly.
Lamentations is described as poems over a ruined city (Jerusalem); no date given. Confirm.
Nehemiah 2:17 is spoken as 'Come, and let us build up the wall' (shortened from 'come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem'); confirm the shortening is acceptable.
Original: בָּנָה (banah, to build) is the dictionary form; the form in Nehemiah 2:18 is וּבָנִינוּ. Confirm the choice.
The question of why God allows disasters is left open on purpose; Keeper may want to name how traditions approach it.

Editor pass: Luke 13:1 has people report Pilate's killing of Galileans; Jesus himself raises the tower in 13:4, so the teach now says so. Cut 'immediate' (Acts 11 gives no timing) and 'rubble still warm'. Keeper note: Jesus goes on, 'except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish' (13:5); the lesson quotes only the refusal to blame the victims.
Audit: garbled sentence about the tower fixed. Keeper note: day 1377 also used the tower in Siloam; here it serves the disaster theme, but the angle (not blaming victims) overlaps.
